Why Im glad Treyarch will let you skip to the end of Black Ops 3
"Why I'm annoyed ArsTechnica still use cheap clickbait titles"
I thought the title itself was descriptive of the content itself. The article is about how you can skip the storyline in Black Ops 3 and why the writer thinks that's a good thing.

Yet it does not tell the reader why the ability to skip through the storyline of BO3 is a good thing. The titles does not tell the reader what the article itself is about - maybe the ability to skip the gameplay is a good thing because the gameplay is bad. Or maybe the author claims its a good thing because he's one of those stupid hipster wankers who crawl all over "muh narrative". At any rate, the headline of an article should reflect its contents, rather than being a surprise bag of what the article may or may not contain.

So it sounds like it may not have the level of detail that you would like (and I'd agree that it should have been improved) but that doesn't mean it's clickbait. The title does still tell the reader what the article will be about and the omission of any details in the title doesn't mislead the reader as to what the writer will be saying.

But that's clickbait in its most basic level: The headline does tell you that <certain subject> is good/garbarge, without actually telling you why this is the case, thus forcing you to actually click the website to find out why the author of the respective article thinks this is the case.

It's like a scientific study whose header tells you that this or that is bad but does not mention whether the author came to this conclusion because he actually studied the subject or whether he is just sputtering bullshit.

But it's an opinion piece. It's not saying "<certain subject> is good/garbage," it's saying "Why I'm glad <certain subject>". The expectation is that the author is going to expand his opinion, which is reflected in the title.

I think a better title would be "I'm glad Treyarch is giving players fuller, easier access to all of the content they purchase" (which is the author's main point) but even that leaves out detail: "how are they giving fuller access, what do you consider fuller access, etc.

The title as written doesn't mislead the reader in any way and doesn't require you to click the link to know what the article is going to be about, which is what I'd consider clickbait.

I would be much easier to give the article merit if the author followed the basic principle of "Because this and that, I feel this and that is the case", rather than simply using a header that tells the reader that "I feel this and that is the case, give me clicks if you want to know why". The idea of clickbait is that the user actually has to click the bait (i.e., the link to the article in question) in order to understand what the author is actually talking about.

I understand where you're coming from, and I do agree that "what because why" is a much better and more straightforward way to title a thesis. But there's a difference between a title that tells you the intent of the article and one that doesn't. You can look at any number of opinion pieces posted in /v/gaming and make the same complaint that you're making here:

"Twitchs hypocritical nudity policy shows its out of touch with the modern world" (well, why does it show that?)

"The Point - Buggy, Rushed Games & Annualized Franchises" (what about them?)

"Do Not Buy Black Ops 3 It Sucks! Just Another Titanfall Clone Without Mechs!" (how so?)

"Regarding Borderlands 2-A Question for Anthony Burch" (what's the question?)

"Hackers and Cheaters In Star Wars Battlefront Already" (how can you tell?)

Not one of these titles follows the "what because why" formula, but they all give an accurate description of the content with varying degrees of detail. You're never going to get the level of detail from a title that you'll get from reading the article. Some titles are better than others, but that doesn't mean lack of detail is clickbait. As long as the title accurately describes the content of the post and doesn't mislead the reader, I don't consider that clickbait at all.

Fair enough. I'm just tired of article (and particularly opinion pieces) whose headlines literally read "A is B and here's why", or "Top 5 Reasons why A is B" when it would be so easy to write "(Imho) A is B because C.

My 2 cents: All the point of a title is is to inform a potential reader of a topic, what it will be about. The reader then actively chooses whether or not to engage based off of the title.

I would classify titles such as "top 10 must know secrets of..." Or something similar to those lines as clickbait, because the actual price arguably doesn't have a thesis, making it more of a news blurb than an actual informative opinion/summary/discussion etc.

That being said "why I think [topic] is a good thing" is not clickbait because it clearly outlines the topic of the arguement and establishes that the following media will be an opinion piece, not some stupid top 10 list or buzzfeed.

Now it's possible to make a mediocre article have an informative title, but that's pretty rare nowadays.
